title: Where HTML Is Made: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR
summary: Compare where and when a page's HTML is made, in the browser, per request, at build time, or regenerated, and what each means for speed and SEO.
intro: Ask a React app's server for a page, and you might get a whole page of HTML, or an empty `<div>` and a script tag. Which one you get decides how soon people see something, whether search engines and link previews can read the page, and what the site costs to run. It comes down to where and when the HTML is made: in the browser, on a server for each visit, once when the site is built, or rebuilt now and then. This lesson explains each of those strategies, the short names teams use for them, CSR, SSR, SSG, and ISR, and which pages each one suits.

steps.title: Two meanings of rendering
steps.body:
People say render and mean two different things. Mixing them up is the fastest way to get lost in any talk about how fast a page is, so this part pulls them apart first.

## Drawing pixels, and making HTML

The first meaning is the one the web course taught: the browser's pipeline. The browser reads HTML into the DOM, works out the styles, lays out every box, and paints pixels. That always happens in the browser, on every page, and nothing in this lesson changes it.

The second meaning is about making the HTML in the first place. In React, to **render** means to call your components to work out what the UI should be: the element tree. When that happens in a browser, React then turns the tree into DOM elements. When it happens anywhere else, React turns the tree into a string of HTML that can be sent to a browser. A **rendering strategy** is a choice of where and when that happens.

## Three moments

HTML can be made at one of three moments:

- **Build time**: when you run the build, like `npm run build`. It happens once, on your computer or on a server that builds your site, before anyone visits.
- **Request time**: when a request reaches a server. It happens again for every visit.
- **Browser time**: after the HTML and JavaScript reach the visitor's browser, on their device.

```diagram rendering-strategies-moments
Each strategy makes the HTML at a different moment, and pages made on a server still hydrate in the browser.
```

Each strategy has a short name, and the diagram places each one at its moment. **SSG**, static site generation, makes every page at build time. **ISR**, incremental static regeneration, does too, then rebuilds pages on a server now and then. **SSR**, server-side rendering, makes each page at request time. **CSR**, client-side rendering, makes it in the browser. The pages a server makes still run React in the browser afterwards, in a step called **hydration**, which the part on SSR explains.

## How to compare them

Recall the web course's measures of a page's speed. Four of them separate these strategies:

- **TTFB**, time to first byte: from asking for the page to the first byte of the answer. It grows when the server has work to do before it answers.
- **FCP**, first contentful paint: when the first text or picture appears, so the screen is no longer blank.
- **LCP**, largest contentful paint: when the biggest thing on the page appears, usually the main picture or heading.
- **INP**, interaction to next paint: how quickly the page shows a response after a click or a tap.

Two more things decide which strategy fits a page.

**SEO**, search engine optimization, means making pages that search engines can find, read, and rank. Search engines read pages with **crawlers**, programs that fetch page after page. Google's crawler runs JavaScript, but it may do that in a second pass, some time later. Many others don't run it at all, including the programs that make **link previews**, the title, text, and picture that appear when you paste a link into a chat. What those programs see is the HTML in the first response, and nothing else.

**Cost** is the other: a page that needs a server to run code for every visit costs more than files a CDN can hand out. Recall that a **CDN**, a content delivery network, is a set of servers around the world that keep copies of files close to the people asking for them.

The rest of this lesson takes the strategies one at a time, in the order teams usually meet them.

steps.title: Client-side rendering
steps.body:
Client-side rendering is what a new Vite React project gives you, so it's where every React developer starts. Knowing exactly what it sends explains both why it's popular and why it isn't enough for every page. ## What gets sent With **CSR**, client-side rendering, the server sends the same small HTML file for every page of the app. It has the page's title, a link to the CSS, a script tag, and one empty element for React to fill: ```html
``` That file is called the **shell**. Everything you'll see on the page is made later, in the browser. ```diagram rendering-strategies-csr Nothing useful appears until step 5, after two downloads and an API call. ``` Follow the diagram. In step 1 the shell arrives, which is fast, since it's tiny and the same for everyone. In step 2 the browser downloads the JavaScript **bundle**, the file the build made from all of your code and React's. In step 3 it runs: React calls your components and builds the DOM inside the root element. But the app has no data yet, so it shows a loading message or a spinner. In step 4 the app asks an API for the data with `fetch`, and waits again. In step 5 the data arrives, React renders again, and the content appears. The first example shows a real shell. The page in it shows a heading and a product with its price, and none of that text is in the HTML. ## What it's good at - **Fast moves after the first load.** Once the bundle is running, going from screen to screen needs no new HTML. React draws the next screen at once and fetches only the data it needs, which the Routing and App Structure lesson builds. - **Cheap, simple hosting.** The build is a folder of files, so any CDN can serve it, with no server code to run or pay for. - **A simple model.** Everything happens in one place, the browser, and every page is made the same way. ## What it costs - **A blank page until the JavaScript runs.** On a fast laptop, steps 1 to 5 take a blink. On a cheap phone on a slow network, downloading and running the bundle can take seconds, and FCP and LCP wait for all of it. - **Weak SEO and link previews.** A crawler that doesn't run JavaScript sees the shell: an empty `
`. A link to a CSR product page, pasted into a chat, previews with no product name and no picture. - **Data starts late.** The request for data can't start until the bundle has downloaded and run, so the two waits happen one after the other instead of at the same time. A chain of waits like that is called a **waterfall**, after the shape the bars make. ## Where it fits CSR fits pages that search engines never see and people use for a long time: a dashboard behind a login, an admin tool, an email inbox, a design tool. There, a second or so at the start doesn't matter much, and the fast moves afterwards do. In Trailhead, the cart and the checkout fit too, since they're private and change with every click.

examples.title: The shell a client-rendered app sends
examples.prompt: A Vite React app whose page shows Trailhead and Trail Pack 45L: $189.00. `npm run build` wrote its HTML to `dist/index.html`, and the server sends that file as it is, so this is what a crawler gets.
examples.explanation: That's the whole file, and everything the server sends for the page. The `<script type="module">` tag loads the bundle, and the `<link>` loads the CSS. Both have a fingerprint in their names, like `jO7qZ66Z`, so browsers can keep them for a long time. And the `<body>` holds one empty `<div id="root">`. The words Trailhead, Trail Pack 45L, and $189.00 appear nowhere, because they don't exist until the bundle runs in a browser and React renders them into that div. A crawler or a link preview that doesn't run JavaScript sees a page called trailhead with nothing in it. Every page of this app, whatever its URL, sends this same file.

steps.title: Server-side rendering and hydration
steps.body:
Server-side rendering puts the content in the very first response, so people see the page, and crawlers read it, without waiting for any JavaScript. It brings a step of its own, hydration, that every React developer runs into sooner or later.

## HTML for every request

With **SSR**, server-side rendering, a server runs your React components for each request. It fetches whatever data the page needs, renders the components to a string of HTML with that data already in it, and sends the whole page. The browser shows it as soon as it arrives, as it would any HTML page, so FCP and LCP come early, and crawlers and link previews get everything. The second example shows the same app as the previous part, rendered this way.

## Hydration

The HTML alone can't respond to anything. The buttons are there, but no listeners are attached, since the components ran on the server, and listeners can't travel in HTML. So the page also loads the same JavaScript bundle as a CSR app. When it runs, React renders the components again, in the browser, and instead of making new DOM it matches its element tree against the HTML that's already there, element by element. Then it attaches the event handlers to the existing elements, and from then on, React runs the page as it would in a CSR app.

That step is **hydration**: React taking over HTML that arrived ready-made, like adding water to something dried. It's why React can't simply keep the HTML and skip rendering in the browser: it needs its own element tree to know which DOM goes with which component.

```diagram rendering-strategies-ssr
The content shows up at step 2, but nothing responds until step 4.
```

Follow the diagram, which uses the same time scale as the CSR one. In step 1 the server fetches the data and renders, before it sends a byte. In step 2 the HTML arrives, and the page is visible. In step 3 the browser downloads the bundle, and in step 4 React hydrates and the page becomes interactive.

## Visible is not the same as ready

Between steps 2 and 4, the page looks finished but doesn't respond. Someone who taps Add to cart in that gap gets nothing, or a plain link or form doing its default thing. On a slow phone the gap can last seconds. That's why SSR doesn't remove the cost of JavaScript: it only moves when people see the page. The ways to shrink the gap, like sending less JavaScript or hydrating the important parts first, come in the last part of this lesson and in the Rendering React on the Server lesson.

For hydration to work, the browser's render has to produce the same tree as the server's. If it doesn't, because a component showed the current time, a random number, or something only the browser knows like the window's width, React warns about a **hydration mismatch**, and may throw the server's HTML away and render from scratch.

## What it costs

- **A server for every request.** Each visit runs your components and fetches data, so you pay for servers that grow with your traffic, and a bug on the server can take down every page.
- **A later first byte.** TTFB now includes the server's work. A slow database means a slow first byte, and the page stays blank until then.
- **Harder caching.** Each response is made fresh, often for one person, so a CDN can't simply hand out copies.

## Where it fits

SSR fits pages that are different for each request and still need to load fast or be found: search results, a page that shows live stock, a news feed made for each reader, an account page that should show its content without a spinner.

examples.title: The same page, rendered on the server
examples.prompt: The app from the previous part, rendered by a small Node server that calls `renderToString` from `react-dom/server` for each request. The Rendering React on the Server lesson builds one. This is what curl got back from it.
examples.output:
Trailhead

Trail Pack 45L: $189.00
examples.explanation: The head is the same as the CSR shell's, script tag and all, since the browser still needs the bundle for hydration. The difference is inside `<div id="root">`: the whole UI is already there, with the heading, the product's name, and its price. A crawler reads it, a link preview shows it, and the browser paints it before any JavaScript runs. The `<!-- -->` pieces are HTML comments React adds between pieces of text that came from different places in the JSX: the product name, the colon, and the price. In HTML, neighboring text runs together, so the markers let hydration match each piece to the text node it came from.

steps.title: Static site generation
steps.body:
Many pages are the same for everyone: a help article, a blog post, a shop's home page. Making that HTML again on every visit is wasted work. Static site generation makes it once, which is the fastest and cheapest way to serve a page.

## Build every page ahead of time

With **SSG**, static site generation, the build renders every page of the site, with its data, and saves each one as an HTML file. Then those files are put on a CDN. When someone asks for a page, the nearest CDN server hands over the file, with no code running for that request. If the page has interactive parts, the bundle loads and React hydrates it, just as after SSR. Making HTML ahead of time like this is also called **prerendering**.

From the outside, an SSG page looks like an SSR page: the content is in the first response. The difference is when the HTML was made: once, at build time, instead of for each request.

## Why it's the fastest

- **The best first byte.** There's no server work at all, and the file is often on a server in the same city as the visitor.
- **The lowest cost.** Serving files from a CDN is cheap, and it costs the same however many people visit.
- **Little to break.** There's no server code to crash and no database to overload when a page suddenly gets popular.
- **Perfect for SEO.** Every page is complete HTML.

The example shows a real one: React's own documentation, react.dev, which is built ahead of time and served from a CDN.

## Where it falls short

- **Stale until the next build.** The HTML is only as fresh as the last build. Change a product's price in the database, and the page shows the old price until someone builds and deploys the site again.
- **Builds grow with the site.** Ten pages build in seconds. A shop with 50,000 products builds 50,000 pages every time, which can take many minutes, even when one price changed.
- **The same page for everyone.** The HTML can't say Hello, Sam, or show what's in your cart. Anything personal has to be filled in by JavaScript in the browser after the page loads, the way CSR does it.

## Where it fits

Docs, blogs, marketing pages, landing pages, and help centers: pages that change when someone publishes, not every minute, and that people find through search. For pages that change more often, the next part keeps SSG's speed and adds a way to refresh them.

examples.title: A statically generated page on a CDN
examples.prompt: Ask react.dev for one of its pages. `-I` asks for the status line and headers only, and `grep` keeps the lines that say where the page came from and how old it is.
examples.output:
HTTP/2 200
age: 884069
cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
server: Vercel
x-vercel-cache: HIT
examples.explanation: `HTTP/2 200` is the status line: the page was found, sent over HTTP/2. `server: Vercel` says who served it: Vercel, a hosting company with its own CDN. `x-vercel-cache: HIT` means the CDN already had a copy and handed it over without running any code for this request, a cache hit. `age: 884069` is how many seconds that copy has been sitting in the cache, about ten days, and every visitor in that time got the same HTML. `cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` tells your browser it may keep a copy too, but must check with the server before reusing it, so a new build reaches people at once. The page itself is complete HTML: its heading, Quick Start, is right there in the response, so crawlers and link previews read it without running any JavaScript.

steps.title: Incremental static regeneration
steps.body:
SSG is fast and cheap, but stale until the next build. For a shop's product pages, where a price or stock changes a few times a day, rebuilding the whole site each time is too slow, and rendering every page on every request is too costly. Incremental static regeneration sits in between.

## Rebuild one page, when it's due

With **ISR**, incremental static regeneration, pages start out static, built ahead of time and served from a cache like SSG pages. But each page can be rebuilt on its own, without a new build of the whole site: after it reaches a certain age, or when you ask. Incremental means one page at a time, as each one needs it.

## Stale while revalidate

The usual way to rebuild after an age is called **stale-while-revalidate**: serve the old copy at once, and fetch a new one in the background. To **revalidate** is to check with the server for a newer version.

```diagram rendering-strategies-isr
Visitor 2 gets the old page at once, and that visit pays for visitor 3's fresh one.
```

Follow the diagram. The page is built at deploy, at 0:00, and stays fresh for 60 seconds. Visitor 1, at 0:30, gets the fresh copy from the cache. At 1:00 the copy goes stale, but nothing happens yet, since nobody asked. Visitor 2, at 1:30, still gets the stale copy, instantly, and that visit starts a rebuild of this one page on the server. Visitor 3, a few seconds later, gets the new page.

Nobody ever waits for a rebuild, and each page is rebuilt at most once a minute, however many people visit. The cost is that someone, here visitor 2, sees a copy up to a little more than a minute old. For a product description, that's fine. For a bank balance, it isn't.

## It's an HTTP header

ISR sounds like a framework feature, and frameworks like Next.js package it, but underneath it's HTTP caching, from the web course's lessons on Cache-Control. The server sends the page with a header like the one in the example. **`s-maxage`** is like `max-age`, but for shared caches like a CDN, not for the browser. **`stale-while-revalidate`** says how long after that the CDN may still serve the old copy while it fetches a new one. Any server behind a CDN that understands these values gets ISR's behavior.

## On demand

Waiting for a page to go stale is fine when you don't know when the data changes. Often you do: someone edits a price in the shop's admin page. **On-demand revalidation** means telling the cache right then to drop that page, or rebuild it, so the next visitor gets the new price without waiting out the time limit. CDNs call dropping a copy a **purge**, and they have an API for it. Frameworks wrap it in one function call, which the Next.js course uses.

## Where it fits

Pages that are the same for everyone but change now and then: product pages in a big shop, news articles that get corrected, listings, event pages. In the Next.js course, Trailhead's product pages work this way.

examples.title: The response that makes a CDN do ISR
examples.prompt: A product page's response, with the Cache-Control header a server sends to let a CDN keep it for a minute, then refresh it in the background for up to five more.
examples.code:
GET /products/trail-pack-45 HTTP/1.1
Host: trailhead.example

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
examples.explanation: `public` lets shared caches like a CDN keep the page at all. `max-age=0` tells the browser not to reuse its own copy without checking, so a person who reloads always asks again. `s-maxage=60` lets the CDN serve its copy, without asking the server, for 60 seconds. `stale-while-revalidate=300` lets it go on serving that copy for up to 300 more seconds while it asks the server for a new one in the background, which is the stale-while-revalidate in the diagram. If nobody visits for more than six minutes, the next visitor waits for a fresh render, since the copy is too old to serve. The body is cut short here: it's the page's whole HTML, rendered on the server.

steps.title: Streaming, islands, and Server Components
steps.body:
The four strategies so far make a whole page one way. Newer techniques mix them inside a single page, so the fast parts don't wait for the slow ones. You'll hear their names in any modern React project, so this part explains each one in brief, and later lessons build them.

## Streaming SSR

A page often has one slow part: a product page's reviews come from a slow service, while everything else is ready at once. Plain SSR waits for the slowest data before it sends a single byte. **Streaming** SSR sends the HTML in pieces as each one is ready. HTTP allows that: a response can arrive bit by bit over one connection. The page's frame, with the header, the product, and the price, arrives at once, with a placeholder like Loading reviews where the slow part goes. When the reviews are ready, the server sends their HTML later in the same response, with a little script that puts it in place. React does this with a component called `Suspense`, which the Rendering React on the Server lesson uses.

## Partial prerendering

**Partial prerendering** combines SSG and streaming in one response. The parts of a page that are the same for everyone, like the layout, the product's description, and its pictures, are built ahead of time and sent from the CDN at once. The parts that can't be, like the stock count or the cart badge, are left as holes, and a server streams them in. You get SSG's first byte and SSR's fresh data on the same page. Next.js does this, and the Next.js course uses it.

## Islands

Many pages are mostly text with a few interactive spots: an article with a comment box, a shop page with an Add to cart button. Hydrating the whole page means sending the JavaScript for all of it, including the parts that never change. The **islands** approach sends plain HTML with no JavaScript for most of the page, and hydrates only the interactive components, the islands. **Astro** is the best known tool built this way, and its islands can be React components.

## React Server Components

**React Server Components** are components that only ever run on the server, at build time or request time. Their code is never sent to the browser, so they add nothing to the bundle, and they can read a database or a file directly, since they're on the server. Components that need the browser, for clicks, state, or effects, are marked as **client components**, and only those are sent and hydrated. One page mixes both. The Rendering React on the Server lesson shows how they work, and Next.js is built around them.

## Choosing, page by page

A real app doesn't pick one strategy. It picks one for each kind of page:

| Page | Strategy | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A docs page or a blog post | SSG | The same for everyone, and changes when someone publishes |
| A shop's home page | SSG or ISR | Mostly the same for everyone, and changes now and then |
| A product page | ISR, with stock streamed in | The same for everyone, but the price and stock change |
| Search results | SSR | Different for every search, and search engines should see them |
| An account page | SSR or CSR | Different for each person, and private |
| The cart and checkout | CSR | Private, and change with every click |
| A dashboard behind a login | CSR | No crawler sees it, and people use it for hours |

The Trailhead you build in this course starts as a CSR app, the way Vite makes it, and that suits most of its screens. In the Rendering React on the Server lesson you'll do the other strategies with React itself, so you see what each one takes, and in the Next.js course, a framework picks among them for each page.

First, though, you need React itself. The next lesson, Components, JSX, and Props, starts writing it.

recap:
- In React, rendering means calling components to make an element tree, which becomes DOM in a browser or an HTML string anywhere else.
- HTML can be made at build time, at request time, or in the browser, and each strategy picks one of those moments.
- CSR sends an empty shell and builds the page in the browser: cheap and quick to move around in, but blank until the JavaScript runs, and weak for SEO.
- SSR renders HTML on a server for each request, then hydration attaches React to it, and between the two the page is visible but not ready.
- SSG builds every page once and serves files from a CDN: the fastest and cheapest, but stale until the next build.
- ISR rebuilds one page at a time after an age or on demand, using HTTP's s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate.
- Streaming, partial prerendering, islands, and Server Components mix strategies inside one page.
- Pick a strategy for each kind of page, by who sees it, how often it changes, and whether crawlers need it.
